doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Coal jobs, retraining, travel and the beauty of many languages
summary: Talk of coal jobs, the need for study and travel, and enjoying languages, which Rowe hears in his music.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Yeah it’s scary. You’d think that the instant communication that we have now would make things better and more truthful and it’s not.

But the thing is people don’t want to hear it. It’s almost like saying to the coal miners that believe those jobs are coming back — if they do come back, they’re going to come back with robots. They’re not coming back, they’re not sending human beings down into those mines anymore. And the whole concept, what Obama was trying to do, he was putting in programs where he had community college programs where these people come and be re- trained for real jobs that were coming in the future. And they rejected that. My father was a coal miner, my grandfather was a coal miner, I’m going to be a coal miner. Yeah you’re going to be a coal miner but there’s no coal miner jobs so you’re going to be a coal miner sitting around with your hat and light on for the rest of your life you know. So these guys rejected re-training for the dream and the fallacy that our new president has put forth saying, “I’m bring these jobs back.” Because he has no idea of the complexity. I mean life is not very very as simple, there’s complex layers and layers and layers of things that need to be taken care of. Life is not simple. And the only way you know about complexity is that you’ve got to do a lot of reading, you’ve got to study, and you just can’t watch one station. You’ve got to go across the gamut, you have to read different papers because different papers have different information. And you have to travel internationally, which most Americans, they say most Americans don’t even have a passport. If you’re not traveling internationally and you’re talking about people in Muslim countries and you’ve never been to a Muslin country in your life, they you’ve got an issue there. That’s a serious problem you know. I mean how could you talk about these people being this and being that, if you’ve never been there. And then this whole thing where women and men come into a restaurant and someone’s speaking in their native tongue and they turn around and say, “Stop that! You’re an American now, speak English.” And I mean how ridiculous. I mean that’s one of the things I love, you know, when you’re traveling internationally and you go to the airport. And you have people, you know, surrounding you, all of them speaking different languages, all the different rhythms, all the different tones and all the nuances and everything. I think that is so beautiful when you have people surrounding you speaking different languages. Even if you don’t understand what they’re saying, just the tones. I guess maybe that’s being a musician, but I’ve found that with other people too. You know I just like it when somebody’s speaking German, somebody’s speaking in French, somebody’s speaking in Spanish, all simultaneously. And you know just those rhythms are just delightful. I love hearing that stuff.
Well I can hear that, now that you say that, I can hear that coming out in your music.
